title: Election, grace and the human will
question: How does God save — election, grace and the human will?
intro:
All the traditions surveyed here agree that salvation is a gift of God's grace in Jesus Christ, that humans are sinners who cannot save themselves, and that faith is necessary. They disagree about how God's eternal choice relates to human response: whether God's election is unconditional or based on foreseen faith, whether grace can be resisted, whether Christ died with the intention of saving every person or a definite people, whether fallen people are able to respond to the gospel, and whether believers can finally fall away.

The debate is ancient (Augustine against Pelagius in the fifth century), was sharpened in the Reformation (Luther against Erasmus, Dort against the Remonstrants, Jesuits against Dominicans), and remains lively today, especially among Baptists and evangelicals. Each position below is presented as its own best advocates would present it, with the strongest objections from the others and the replies they give.

positions.name: Calvinism (Reformed monergism)
positions.summary:
Calvinism holds that fallen humans are unable, by their own powers, to turn to God, so salvation depends entirely on God's sovereign initiative. Before creation God unconditionally chose a definite people in Christ; Christ's death secures their redemption; the Holy Spirit effectually regenerates them so that they freely and willingly believe; and God preserves them to the end.

The position is usually summarised by the later acronym TULIP (Total depravity, Unconditional election, Limited or particular atonement, Irresistible or effectual grace, Perseverance of the saints), which tracks the five heads of doctrine of the Synod of Dort (1618–1619). Its defenders stress that this framework gives God all the glory, grounds assurance in God's purpose rather than human resolve, and is the most natural reading of Romans 8–9, Ephesians 1 and John 6.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.profession: Bishop of Hippo, theologian
figures.bio: North African bishop whose controversy with Pelagius and his followers produced the Western church's classic doctrines of original sin, the necessity of prevenient and operative grace, and gratuitous predestination. His late anti-Pelagian works argue that both the beginning of faith and perseverance are gifts given to the elect. Later Calvinists regarded him as their chief patristic forebear, though he also held views (on baptismal regeneration and the possibility of regenerate people not persevering) that Reformed theology does not share.

works.author: Augustine
works.title: On the Predestination of the Saints

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.profession: Reformer and pastor in Geneva
figures.bio: French humanist-trained reformer who led the church in Geneva. His *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, expanded from 1536 to its final Latin edition of 1559, treats election and reprobation in the context of the Christian life and assurance rather than as a starting axiom. He taught that God's eternal decree chose some to life and passed over others, and called the decree of reprobation awe-inspiring yet just. His biblical commentaries remain widely used.

works.author: John Calvin
works.title: Concerning the Eternal Predestination of God

figures.name: Theodore Beza
figures.profession: Calvin's successor in Geneva, professor of theology
figures.bio: Beza led the Genevan Academy after Calvin and gave Reformed predestination a more tightly ordered, scholastic presentation, including a chart of the order of the divine decrees. He is often associated with supralapsarianism and with the doctrine of definite atonement. Jacobus Arminius studied under him in Geneva before later breaking with this system.

figures.name: John Owen
figures.profession: English Puritan pastor, theologian, Oxford vice-chancellor
figures.bio: The most influential English Puritan theologian. His *Death of Death in the Death of Christ* is the classic defence of particular redemption, arguing that Christ's death actually accomplishes salvation for those for whom it was intended rather than making salvation merely possible. He also wrote a polemic against Arminianism and major works on the Holy Spirit and communion with God.

works.title: The Death of Death in the Death of Christ

figures.name: R. C. Sproul
figures.profession: Presbyterian theologian, founder of Ligonier Ministries
figures.bio: American teacher whose books, lectures and radio broadcasts did much to spread Reformed soteriology among late-twentieth-century evangelicals. His *Chosen by God* explains predestination for lay readers, emphasising regeneration preceding faith and the holiness of God.

positions.context: The position grew out of Augustine's fifth-century conflict with Pelagianism and was revived in the sixteenth century by the magisterial Reformers, all of whom (Luther included) taught the bondage of the will. In the Reformed churches it was refined in debate: after Arminius's followers issued the Remonstrance (1610), the international Synod of Dort (1618–1619) answered with the Canons of Dort, whose five heads of doctrine are the basis of the later TULIP acronym (the acronym itself is modern, attested only from the early twentieth century). The Westminster Confession (1646) and the London Baptist Confession (1689) embedded the doctrine in Presbyterian and Particular Baptist churches. English and American Puritans, the evangelical leader George Whitefield, Jonathan Edwards, Charles Spurgeon, and the twentieth-century 'new Calvinism' associated with figures such as J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul and John Piper carried it into the modern era.
claims: 1. Total depravity: sin affects every part of the person, so that no one, left to themselves, will or can come to God in saving faith (not that people are as wicked as possible).
2. Unconditional election: before creation God chose particular people for salvation in Christ, not because he foresaw their faith or merit but according to his own good pleasure.
3. Particular (definite) redemption: Christ's death was intended to secure and actually accomplish the salvation of the elect, while being sufficient in worth for all and sincerely offered to all.
4. Effectual (irresistible) grace: the Spirit regenerates the elect so that they freely come to Christ; outward calls can be and are resisted, but God's inward call infallibly achieves its purpose.
5. Perseverance of the saints: those whom God has truly regenerated will be kept by God and will continue in faith to the end, though they may fall seriously for a time.
6. Compatibilism: God's decree and genuine human choice are both real; humans act willingly and are responsible, though their choices are certain under God's providence.

scriptures.reading: God chose Jacob over Esau before either had done good or evil, so that his purpose of election would stand; mercy depends on God who shows it, not on human will or effort. Read as individual election to salvation.
The Father chose believers in Christ before the foundation of the world and predestined them to adoption according to the purpose of his will, which works all things according to his counsel.

All whom the Father gives to the Son will come; no one can come unless the Father draws him, and every one who is drawn is raised up on the last day. The drawing is therefore effectual, not merely enabling.
As many as were appointed to eternal life believed: appointment precedes and explains faith.
The golden chain: those foreknown (known in covenant love) are predestined, called, justified and glorified, with no one lost between links.
Jesus tells his opponents they do not believe because they are not his sheep, implying belonging precedes believing.
Humans are dead in sin until God makes them alive with Christ; faith and salvation are God’s gift so that no one may boast.
The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, a particular people (compare John 10:15 and John 17:9).
God who began the good work will bring it to completion, grounding perseverance in God’s faithfulness.

arguments.text: The clearest passages on election (Romans 9, Ephesians 1, John 6) ground salvation in God's choice prior to and independent of human response, and Paul anticipates the objection 'is God unjust?', which would only arise if election were unconditional.
Scripture describes the unregenerate as dead, blind, hostile to God and unable to submit to him, so faith must be the fruit of regeneration rather than its cause.
If two people receive the same grace and one believes while the other does not, the deciding factor lies in the human; this gives grounds for boasting, which Paul excludes.

If Christ's death paid for the sins of all people without exception, either all must be saved or God punishes some sins twice; a definite atonement avoids both by tying Christ's intention to its effect.

Divine foreknowledge of future free acts already makes them certain; Arminian foreknowledge therefore does not remove the difficulty it is meant to solve, whereas a decree explains why the future is certain.

Augustine's anti-Pelagian theology was received by the Western church (Council of Orange, 529, condemned the idea that the beginning of faith comes from human nature), and all the magisterial Reformers affirmed unconditional election in some form.
Assurance and perseverance rest on God's keeping power, which no external power can overturn.

critiques.text: John 3:16 says God so loved the world that whoever believes may have life; this universal love and offer seems incompatible with a decree that leaves most of the world without any provision.
1 Tim 2:4 says God desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. If God unconditionally elects only some, his stated desire is frustrated by his own decree.
2 Pet 3:9 says the Lord is not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance. This expresses a universal saving will.
1 John 2:2 says Christ is the propitiation not only for our sins but for the sins of the whole world, contradicting limited atonement.

Ezek 18:23 and 18:32 (and 33:11) declare that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn and live. A God who passes over people whom he could save appears to contradict this.
In Matt 23:37 Jesus says he often wished to gather Jerusalem's children 'and you would not'. This shows grace can be successfully resisted and that God's desire can be thwarted by human refusal.
Heb 2:9 says Jesus tasted death for everyone, which seems to extend the atonement to every person.
1 Tim 4:10 calls God the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe. This implies a saving relationship to all that is distinct from, but not opposed to, his relation to believers.
Titus 2:11 says the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people, which fits prevenient grace extended to everyone.
Acts 7:51 has Stephen charge his hearers: you always resist the Holy Spirit. Grace is therefore resistible.
Heb 6:4-6 describes people who were enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit and then fell away. This seems to deny unconditional perseverance.
Rom 11:32 says God has consigned all to disobedience in order that he may have mercy on all. The climax of Romans 9–11 is universal mercy, not selective decree.
Deut 30:19 calls Israel to choose life. A genuine summons to choose implies an ability to respond; otherwise the command is meaningless.
2 Pet 2:1 speaks of false teachers denying the Master who bought them and bringing destruction on themselves, which implies Christ's purchase extends to some who perish.
John 12:32: Jesus will draw all people to himself when lifted up. If 'draw' in John 6:44 is effectual, John 12:32 would teach universalism; so the drawing must be resistible.
1 Cor 8:11 and Rom 14:15 warn that a brother 'for whom Christ died' may be destroyed or ruined, which seems inconsistent with both limited atonement and perseverance.
Luke 7:30 says the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God's purpose for themselves. If God's purpose can be rejected, his will is not always effectual.

Calvinism appears to make God the author of sin: if he determines all things, including the fall and every evil choice, it is hard to see how creatures rather than God bear the blame. Middle knowledge preserves sovereignty without such determinism.

Lutheran theology rejects double predestination and the doctrine of definite atonement as rational speculation beyond the revealed promises. The Formula of Concord (Article XI) warns against inferring reprobation from election and directs consciences to Christ in Word and sacrament.

From the Orthodox standpoint the Augustinian framework (inherited guilt, a will so bound that grace must work monergistically) is a Western innovation, foreign to the Greek fathers, who uniformly taught cooperation between divine grace and human freedom.

Calvinism reads the 'dead in sin' metaphor as total inability, but in Scripture spiritual death means separation, and the same Ephesians 2 passage says believers are saved 'through faith', placing faith logically before being made alive.
If God unconditionally decrees who will be saved, the universal offer of the gospel seems insincere, since God offers to the non-elect what he has not intended for them.

responses.text: Calvinists commonly read 'world' in John as the fallen human order in its rebellion, so the verse magnifies the greatness of God's love for sinners rather than counting every individual; the promise is genuinely to 'whoever believes', and that offer is sincerely made to all. Others (e.g. Amyraldians, or Calvinists such as D. A. Carson) affirm that God has a real general love for all humanity alongside a particular, saving love for the elect.

Two Calvinist replies are common. Some (following Augustine and Owen) read 'all people' as all kinds of people, in context of praying for kings and those in authority (1 Tim 2:1-2). Others (e.g. John Piper in *Are There Two Wills in God?*) accept that 'all' means every person and distinguish God's preceptive will (what he commands and delights in) from his decretive will (what he ordains), noting that every theology must say God permits what he does not desire.

Many Calvinists note that the letter addresses 'you' (believers) and that God is patient toward 'you', so the 'any' may refer to the elect yet to be gathered before the end. Others accept the universal sense and appeal again to the distinction between what God desires in itself and what he wills to bring about.

Owen and many later Calvinists argue 'the whole world' contrasts John's readers with believers among all peoples, echoing John 11:51-52 where Christ dies to gather God's scattered children. Others (e.g. hypothetical universalists within the Reformed tradition) affirm a universal sufficiency and a real offer grounded in the cross while maintaining a special intention for the elect.

Calvin himself commented on Ezekiel 18 by distinguishing God's will as revealed in the call to repentance, which is sincere, from his secret counsel. Calvinists hold that God genuinely delights in repentance and does not delight in death as such, yet may permit and ordain the just judgement of sinners for wider purposes, much as a judge can lament a sentence he justly passes.

Calvinists observe that Jesus addresses the leaders of Jerusalem ('you would not') who prevented 'your children' from being gathered, and they agree that the outward call is resisted constantly. What Calvinism denies is that the Spirit's inward regenerating work fails. The lament also shows Christ's real sorrow over unbelief, which Calvinists affirm.

Many Calvinists point out that the following verses define the 'everyone' as the 'many sons' brought to glory, the 'brothers' and 'the children God has given me' (Heb 2:10-13), so the scope is all of Christ's people. Others accept a universal reference to the sufficiency of his death.

Calvinists commonly take 'Saviour' here in the broader sense of preserver and benefactor (common grace), with 'especially' marking the unique, eternal salvation of believers; some take 'especially' as 'namely'. Either reading avoids universal saving intention.

Calvinists read 'all people' in light of the preceding instructions to older men, women, young men and slaves (Titus 2:1-10): the grace of God has appeared for every class of person. They also note the grace in view trains believers in godliness (Titus 2:12), which describes saving grace already received rather than a universal enabling.

Calvinists agree that the Spirit's work through the external word, prophets and providence is resisted by sinful people all the time; that is what total depravity predicts. The doctrine of effectual calling concerns the Spirit's regenerating work in the heart, which changes the will so that it no longer resists (Ezek 36:26).

Calvinist interpreters offer several readings: (a) the passage describes people who experienced the blessings of the covenant community without genuine regeneration, contrasted with the 'better things that belong to salvation' in Heb 6:9; (b) it is a hypothetical warning God uses as a means to keep the elect persevering. Either way, 1 John 2:19 shows that those who depart reveal they were never truly of the believing community.

Calvinists read Romans 11 as dealing with Jews and Gentiles as groups in redemptive history: both have been shut up under disobedience so that both receive mercy on the same footing. The 'all' corresponds to both peoples, not every individual, since the chapter itself distinguishes the elect remnant from the hardened (Rom 11:5-7).

Calvinists answer that a command reveals duty, not ability (Rom 3:20); Deut 30:6 within the same chapter promises that God will circumcise hearts so that Israel can love him, which is the new-covenant fulfilment Calvinists see in regeneration. God's commands are also the means by which the Spirit works faith in the elect.

Calvinists note that the verse draws on Deut 32:6, where God 'bought' Israel as a nation, and that Peter describes how the false teachers professed to belong to the Lord; the language is that of covenant profession rather than a statement of the atonement's saving intent.

Calvinists point to the setting: Greeks have just asked to see Jesus (John 12:20-23), so 'all' means people of all nations, Jew and Gentile, not every individual. On that reading the drawing remains effectual for those drawn.

Calvinists commonly understand 'destroyed' here as serious spiritual harm or the damage to a weaker believer's faith that Paul warns against, and they treat the language as a description of covenant members in the judgement of charity; the warnings themselves are means by which God preserves his people.
Calvinists answer that 'purpose' (boulē) here refers to God's counsel expressed in John's baptism, his revealed will that they obeyed or refused, not his eternal decree.

The Westminster Confession (3.1) says God ordains whatever comes to pass yet so that he is not the author of sin and the liberty of second causes is established. Calvinists point to texts in which God ordains evil acts for good purposes while the agents remain guilty (Gen 50:20; Acts 2:23; Acts 4:27-28), and argue that Molinism faces a parallel question since God knowingly actualises a world in which specific people sin and perish.

Calvinists answer that they too warn against prying into the secret decree and direct believers to Christ (Calvin called Christ the mirror of election), but hold that Scripture itself speaks of God's choosing some and hardening others (Rom 9:18), so silence on reprobation would be less than biblical.

Calvinists acknowledge Greek patristic emphasis on free will, but argue that many Fathers were opposing pagan fatalism and Gnostic determinism rather than addressing the Pelagian question, and that Scripture, not consensus of a subset of Fathers, is the final norm.

Calvinists answer that Eph 2:5 says God made us alive while we were dead, which is God's act, and that the grammar of 2:8 most naturally treats the whole salvation package, including faith, as God's gift; John 1:13 and 1 John 5:1 tie new birth to God's will and place it before believing.

Calvinists hold that the offer is sincere because every hearer who believes will certainly be saved and the offer reflects God's real delight in repentance. Faithful Reformed preaching has historically been fervently evangelistic (Whitefield, Spurgeon, William Carey).

strawMen.strawMan: Calvinists believe God drags unwilling people into heaven kicking and screaming.
strawMen.correction: Reformed theology teaches that regeneration renews the will so that people come to Christ freely and gladly; 'irresistible' means effectual, not coercive (Canons of Dort 3/4.11–12).

strawMen.strawMan: Calvinism makes evangelism pointless.
strawMen.correction: Calvinists believe God ordains means as well as ends, so preaching is the instrument by which he calls the elect; historic Calvinists founded major missionary movements (e.g. William Carey's Baptist Missionary Society, 1792).

strawMen.strawMan: Calvinists deny human choice and responsibility.
strawMen.correction: The Westminster Confession (ch. 9) affirms that humans have natural liberty and act willingly; Calvinism is compatibilist, not fatalist, and holds people fully accountable for their sin.

positive: Grounds assurance in God's faithfulness rather than human performance.
Fosters humility and doxology: salvation is all of grace.
Produced a large body of rigorous exegesis, confessions and catechisms (Westminster, Heidelberg, 1689).
Historically fuelled missions and revival preaching (Whitefield, Edwards, Carey, Spurgeon).
negative: Can produce anxiety about whether one is elect, a recurring pastoral problem in Puritan history.
Hyper-Calvinist fringes have at times discouraged free offers of the gospel.
Critics argue it raises acute theodicy problems and can portray God as arbitrary.
Debates over TULIP have divided congregations and denominations, notably in modern Baptist life.

adherents: Augustine (in his late works) and the medieval Augustinian tradition (Gottschalk, Thomas Bradwardine, Gregory of Rimini) in related forms
Reformed and Presbyterian churches (Westminster Confession, Three Forms of Unity)
Particular Baptists and Reformed Baptists (Second London Confession, 1689)
Puritans such as William Perkins, John Owen, Thomas Goodwin
George Whitefield, Jonathan Edwards, Charles Spurgeon
Modern figures: J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul, John Piper, Timothy Keller, Thomas Schreiner
Today: PCA, OPC, Reformed churches worldwide, a significant minority in the Southern Baptist Convention, many churches in Korea, Africa and Latin America

positions.name: Arminianism (evangelical synergism)
positions.summary:
Arminianism agrees with Calvinism that fallen humans cannot turn to God unaided, but holds that God, by prevenient (enabling) grace given through the gospel and the Spirit, restores to all who hear the ability to believe or refuse. God elects to salvation those who believe in Christ: either individuals whose faith he foreknows, or Christ and the body of believers as a corporate people. Christ died for every person, grace can be resisted, and (in classical Arminianism) a believer can finally fall away by abandoning faith.

Its defenders stress that this account best honours God's universal love, the sincerity of the gospel offer, and genuine moral responsibility, while still attributing salvation wholly to grace.

figures.name: Jacobus Arminius
figures.profession: Dutch Reformed pastor and Leiden professor
figures.bio: Trained at Leiden and in Geneva under Beza, Arminius became a pastor in Amsterdam and professor at Leiden. Studying Romans 7 and 9 he came to doubt the Reformed doctrine of unconditional reprobation. He affirmed total depravity and the necessity of grace, but taught that God elects believers in Christ, foreknowing who will believe, and that grace can be resisted. He died before the controversy reached its climax.

works.author: Jacobus Arminius
works.title: Examination of Perkins’s Pamphlet on Predestination

figures.name: Simon Episcopius
figures.profession: Remonstrant theologian, leader at the Synod of Dort
figures.bio: Leading spokesman of the Remonstrants, who were expelled from the Synod of Dort. He drafted the Remonstrant Confession and later taught at the Remonstrant seminary in Amsterdam, giving Arminian theology a systematic shape.

figures.name: John Wesley
figures.profession: Anglican priest, founder of Methodism
figures.bio: Evangelist whose preaching and organisation of Methodist societies spread an evangelical Arminianism across Britain and North America. He emphasised prevenient grace, universal atonement, assurance by the witness of the Spirit and growth toward entire sanctification, and broke with George Whitefield over predestination.

figures.name: Roger E. Olson
figures.profession: Baptist theologian and historian, Baylor University
figures.bio: Contemporary evangelical historian whose books correct common misunderstandings of Arminianism, arguing that classical Arminianism is a theology of grace rooted in the Reformation, not semi-Pelagianism.

positions.context: Arminianism arose inside the Dutch Reformed church. After Arminius's death his followers presented the Five Articles of the Remonstrance (1610) to the States of Holland, arguing for conditional election, universal atonement, the necessity of grace, resistible grace and an open question about perseverance. The national Synod of Dort (1618–1619) condemned them, and Remonstrant ministers were deposed; the political turmoil included the execution of the statesman Oldenbarnevelt. Arminian ideas found later homes in the Church of England (the 'Laudian' party), among the General Baptists, and above all in Wesleyan Methodism, whose missionary success made Arminian soteriology dominant in much of global evangelicalism, Pentecostalism and the Holiness movement.
claims: 1. Depravity and inability: apart from grace no one can think, will or do anything truly good or turn to God.
2. Prevenient grace: God gives grace, through the Spirit and the word, that frees the will enough to respond to the gospel; this grace precedes and enables faith but can be resisted.
3. Conditional election: God chooses for salvation those who are in Christ through faith, either foreknown individual believers or the corporate body of believers.
4. Universal atonement: Christ died for every person, making salvation truly available to all, though only believers receive its benefits.
5. Resistible grace: God's saving call can be refused, so those who perish do so by their own culpable rejection.

6. Conditional security (classical view): believers are kept by God through faith, and only those who persist in faith are saved; apostasy is a real possibility (many modern Arminian Baptists hold eternal security instead).

scriptures.reading: God loves the whole world and gives his Son so that whoever believes will have life: a universal love and an open condition.
God desires all people to be saved, and Christ gave himself as a ransom for all.
The Lord is patient, not wanting any to perish but all to come to repentance.
Christ is the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world, not only for believers.
Christ draws all people to himself: the drawing of John 6:44 is extended to all and is therefore enabling rather than irresistible.
Stephen’s hearers always resisted the Holy Spirit, showing that the Spirit’s gracious work can be resisted.
Believers are elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father: election follows foreknowledge.
Genuine believers who have shared in the Spirit are warned that falling away is possible and disastrous.
The grace of God has appeared bringing salvation to all people: a picture of universal prevenient grace.

arguments.text: Many texts express God's desire for the salvation of every person and Christ's death for all, which most naturally implies that the gospel offer is backed by real provision for each hearer.
Moral responsibility requires that a person could have done otherwise; if those who perish could never have believed, it is difficult to see how they are justly condemned for unbelief.
If God determines all things, including sin, it is hard to avoid making him the author of evil; resistible grace locates the cause of damnation solely in the creature.
Scripture repeatedly describes people resisting God's gracious initiatives, and God lamenting this, which presupposes that grace is resistible.
Election in Paul is 'in Christ' (Eph 1:4); believers share Christ's election by union with him through faith, just as Israel was elected as a people.
Pre-Augustinian Fathers, Greek and Latin, generally affirmed free will and conditional election based on foreknowledge, which suggests unconditional election was a later development.
The New Testament's warnings against apostasy are addressed to real believers and assume a real danger.

critiques.text: Romans 9 says election is not of works and does not depend on human will or effort but on God who has mercy, and Paul answers the charge of injustice by appeal to God's freedom as potter, which fits unconditional, not conditional, election.
Ephesians 1:4-11 roots election in God's will and purpose before creation and says he works all things after the counsel of his will, leaving no room for election conditioned on foreseen faith.
John 6:37-44: all whom the Father gives come, no one can come unless drawn, and the one drawn is raised up. Drawing therefore guarantees coming and resurrection.
Acts 13:48 says 'as many as were appointed to eternal life believed', placing appointment before faith.
Rom 8:29-30 presents an unbroken chain from foreknowledge to glorification; everyone predestined is called and justified, so calling must be effectual.
John 10:26: 'you do not believe because you are not my sheep.' Belonging to Christ's flock precedes and explains believing.
If grace is given equally to all and the difference between believer and unbeliever lies in a human choice, believers have something to boast about.
John 6:65 and Phil 1:29 present faith itself as granted by God, not merely made possible.

Simple foreknowledge gives God no providential advantage: if God only knows what will in fact happen, he cannot use that knowledge to plan the world, since it already includes his own actions. Arminianism needs middle knowledge to make sense of sovereignty.

Prevenient grace, as a universal inner enabling distinct from the gospel itself, is not explicitly taught in Scripture; it was introduced to rescue total depravity, which the Bible does not teach in its Augustinian form.

By making election depend on foreseen faith, Arminianism turns God's gracious choice into a response to something in the human being, undermining the comfort of election that the Formula of Concord locates purely in God's mercy (intuitu fidei was rejected by many Lutherans).

Orthodox theologians are sympathetic to Arminian synergy but argue that it remains captive to the Western, juridical framework of guilt and forensic justification, and that 'decision' language can reduce salvation to a moment of choice rather than a lifelong participation in God.
Arminianism cannot guarantee that anyone will be saved: if every person can resist grace, Christ's death might theoretically have saved no one.

responses.text: Arminian exegetes (e.g. Brian Abasciano, building on older readings) argue that Romans 9 addresses God's right to define his covenant people by faith rather than ethnicity or works (Rom 9:30-32), that Jacob and Esau stand for nations (Gen 25:23; Mal 1:2-3), and that the potter imagery from Jer 18 describes a potter who reshapes his vessels in response to their repentance.

Arminians reply that the chapter speaks of being chosen 'in him', so election is christocentric and corporate: God predestined that those in Christ would be adopted, and people come to be in Christ by believing (Eph 1:13). God's sovereign will includes his decision to save through faith.

Arminians note that the 'raise him up' clause may refer to 'the one who comes' rather than every one drawn, that John 12:32 says Christ draws all people, and that John 6:45 explains the drawing as hearing and learning from the Father, which invites but does not compel. The 'given' in John 6:37 can refer to faithful Jews already belonging to the Father under the old covenant who were given to Jesus.

Arminians observe that the verb (tetagmenoi) can be read as middle voice, 'as many as were disposed (or ordered themselves) toward eternal life', contrasting with the Jews who judged themselves unworthy in 13:46. Even on a passive reading, Luke does not specify the basis of appointment.

Arminians read 'foreknew' as foreknowledge of people as believers (or of the church as a people), and note that the chain describes those who love God (8:28), so it states God's purpose for believers rather than a decree about how unbelievers become believers. Wesley read it as describing the order of God's dealings with those who persevere.

Arminians reply that Jesus is addressing hardened opponents who had persistently rejected him (John 10:24-25); being 'not his sheep' describes their present character resulting from their prior refusal, not an eternal decree, and the same context invites them to believe the works (10:37-38).

Arminians answer that receiving a gift is not meritorious: a beggar who accepts bread cannot boast of having earned it. Faith is the empty hand, and Paul himself contrasts faith with works precisely because faith excludes boasting (Rom 3:27).

Arminians agree faith is a gift in the sense that it is possible only by grace; but a gift can be offered and refused. Phil 1:29 also says suffering is 'granted', which no one takes to be irresistibly imposed apart from the person's participation.

Many Arminians accept this and adopt Molinism (e.g. Arminius himself has been read as using middle knowledge). Others reply that God's sovereignty consists in his wise response to free creatures, and that Scripture's emphasis is on God's faithfulness and power, not on a theory of how foreknowledge works.

Arminians respond that John 1:9, John 12:32, John 16:8 and Titus 2:11 point to a universal work of Christ and the Spirit enlightening and convicting people, and that without such grace provisionism risks Semi-Pelagianism by locating the first move toward God in unaided human nature.

Arminians reply that faith is not a work but the means of receiving grace, and that Lutherans themselves teach resistible grace and universal atonement; Arminians simply apply the same logic consistently to election instead of leaving it as a paradox.

Arminians, particularly Wesleyans, reply that Wesley drew on Eastern sources (e.g. he read Macarius) and emphasised sanctification and the real transformation of believers, so the Wesleyan tradition already integrates participation and growth into its understanding of salvation.

Arminians respond that God's foreknowledge assures that many will believe, and Scripture promises a great multitude (Rev 7:9); the certainty of the outcome rests in God's knowledge and promise, even though not in causal determination.

strawMen.strawMan: Arminians believe people save themselves by their own free will.
strawMen.correction: Classical Arminianism affirms total depravity and teaches that no one can believe without God's prevenient grace (Remonstrance, Article 3); salvation is by grace through faith.

strawMen.strawMan: Arminianism is just Pelagianism or Semi-Pelagianism.
strawMen.correction: Pelagius denied the need for inward grace, and Semi-Pelagians held that people could initiate faith; Arminius and Wesley explicitly held that grace must take the initiative.

strawMen.strawMan: Arminians deny God's sovereignty and omniscience.
strawMen.correction: Classical Arminians affirm exhaustive divine foreknowledge and sovereignty; they hold that God sovereignly chose to create free creatures and to save through faith. (Open theism, which denies exhaustive foreknowledge, is a distinct later view.)

positive: Supports a universal, urgent evangelistic message and has driven Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal missions.
Gives a straightforward account of God's universal love and the sincerity of the gospel offer.
Emphasises moral responsibility and holiness of life.
negative: Critics argue it can make assurance depend on the believer's continued performance.
Popular forms can slide toward decisionism or Semi-Pelagianism.
The coherence of libertarian freedom with foreknowledge remains philosophically contested.

adherents: Remonstrant Brotherhood (Netherlands)
John and Charles Wesley and the Methodist movement
General Baptists and Free Will Baptists
Holiness churches (Church of the Nazarene, Wesleyan Church, Salvation Army)
Most Pentecostal denominations (Assemblies of God, Church of God)
Many Anglicans since the seventeenth century

positions.name: Molinism (middle knowledge)
positions.summary:
Molinism holds that God possesses 'middle knowledge': knowledge, logically prior to his decision to create, of what every possible free creature would freely do in every possible set of circumstances. Using this knowledge God chooses to actualise a world in which his purposes are infallibly achieved through, not in spite of, genuinely (libertarian) free choices.

Applied to salvation, God's election is his choice to create a world in which particular people freely respond to his grace; predestination is real and specific, yet nobody is determined to believe or to reject. Molinists argue this combines a strong doctrine of providence with a strong doctrine of human freedom and God's universal salvific will.

figures.name: Luis de Molina
figures.profession: Spanish Jesuit theologian, professor at Évora
figures.bio: Jesuit who developed the theory of scientia media (middle knowledge) to reconcile grace, foreknowledge, providence and free will. His *Concordia* sparked a long and bitter dispute with Dominican Thomists (notably Domingo Báñez), leading to the papal Congregatio de Auxiliis, which ended in 1607 without condemning either side.

works.author: Luis de Molina
works.title: Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis

figures.name: Alvin Plantinga
figures.profession: Analytic philosopher of religion (Calvin College, Notre Dame)
figures.bio: Plantinga's free will defence against the logical problem of evil relied on counterfactuals of freedom, effectively reviving Molina's concept in analytic philosophy, and he later acknowledged the connection.

figures.name: Thomas P. Flint
figures.profession: Philosopher, University of Notre Dame
figures.bio: Catholic philosopher whose book is the standard systematic statement of the Molinist account of providence in contemporary philosophy.

figures.name: William Lane Craig
figures.profession: Philosopher, theologian and apologist
figures.bio: Evangelical apologist who has done more than anyone to introduce Molinism to Protestant audiences, applying it to providence, the problem of evil, biblical prophecy and the question of those who never hear the gospel.

figures.name: Kenneth Keathley
figures.profession: Baptist theologian, Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Keathley applied Molinism directly to soteriology, replacing TULIP with the acronym ROSES (Radical depravity, Overcoming grace, Sovereign election, Eternal life, Singular redemption) and arguing that grace is 'overcoming' though resistible because God's grace works until a person refuses.

works.author: Kenneth Keathley
works.title: Salvation and Sovereignty: A Molinist Approach

positions.context: Molinism emerged in Counter-Reformation Catholicism during the De Auxiliis controversy between Jesuits and Dominicans over how efficacious grace relates to free will, a Catholic parallel to the Protestant debates that culminated at Dort. Arminius may have read Molina and used similar ideas, though how much is debated. After centuries of relative neglect in Protestantism, Molinism was revived in analytic philosophy of religion in the 1970s (Plantinga) and popularised among evangelicals by W. L. Craig. It is attractive to some Baptists and others who want a high view of providence without Calvinist determinism.
claims: 1. God has three logical moments of knowledge: natural knowledge (all possibilities), middle knowledge (what free creatures would do in any circumstances), and free knowledge (what will actually happen, given his decree).
2. Human beings have libertarian freedom with respect to responding to grace; no prior condition determines whether they will believe.
3. God chose to create a world, among those feasible given creaturely freedom, in which his purposes, including the salvation of particular people, are accomplished.
4. Election is therefore specific and certain, yet not causally determining: the elect freely believe, and the lost freely reject grace sufficient for salvation.
5. Christ died for all and God sincerely desires the salvation of all; God may arrange circumstances so that the maximum number of people freely respond.
6. God is the author of the world's providential order but not of sin, because he does not cause free choices, he only permits them knowing what they will be.

scriptures.reading: God tells David that Saul would come and the men of Keilah would surrender him if he stayed; David leaves and neither happens. God knows true conditionals about what free agents would do.
Jesus says Tyre, Sidon and Sodom would have repented if they had seen his works: knowledge of counterfactuals about free human responses.
Christ was delivered up by God’s definite plan and foreknowledge, yet killed by lawless hands: providence working through free, culpable acts.
Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and Israel did what God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place, illustrating sovereign planning that does not cancel culpability.
God determined the times and places of peoples so that they would seek him: providential arrangement of circumstances with a view to free response.
Had the rulers understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory: another true counterfactual of freedom woven into God’s plan.
A person plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps: human planning and divine direction both real.
God desires all to be saved; middle knowledge lets God pursue this desire within the constraints of what free creatures would do.

arguments.text: Scripture attributes to God knowledge of what free creatures would do in circumstances that never occur, which is precisely middle knowledge.
Middle knowledge allows God to exercise meticulous providence without causally determining choices, so he can be sovereign without being the author of sin.

It explains how God can both truly desire everyone's salvation and specifically elect those who will be saved: God chooses among feasible worlds, perhaps one with an optimal balance of saved and lost.
Texts that join divine determination with human guilt, such as the crucifixion narratives, are best explained by a God who decrees through foreseen free acts.
Simple foreknowledge does not help God plan; middle knowledge does, giving the Arminian concern for freedom a robust account of providence.

Molina's view received an extended hearing in the Catholic Church and was never condemned (Congregatio de Auxiliis, ended 1607), and it independently resurfaced in Plantinga's free will defence, suggesting conceptual power.

critiques.text: The grounding objection: what makes counterfactuals of libertarian freedom true before the person exists or decides? If nothing grounds them, they cannot be known. (Raised by Robert Adams and William Hasker, among others.)

Molinism does not avoid the hard questions it accuses Calvinism of: God still knowingly creates a world in which specific people will be lost, and chooses not to create a world in which they would have been saved.

Some Arminians (e.g. Roger Olson) worry that Molinism collapses into a form of determinism: if God selects the world precisely to produce particular choices, the creature's freedom seems a mere instrument in a deterministic plan.

Molinism is a philosophical theory imported to resolve an exegetical debate. Scripture nowhere describes a logical sequence of divine knowledges, and ordinary believers should not need speculative metaphysics to understand salvation.

Lutheran theology warns against speculating about the hidden God (Deus absconditus) and directs faith to God revealed in Christ; Molinism tries to explain what Luther and the Formula of Concord deliberately leave as mystery.

Orthodox theologians see Molinism as a product of Western scholasticism that treats God's knowledge in rationalistic, quasi-temporal stages and focuses on decrees rather than on communion and participation in God.

The proof-texts do not establish middle knowledge: 1 Sam 23 can be read as God's knowledge of Saul's and the Keilahites' settled intentions, and Matt 11:21 as hyperbole; neither need involve libertarian freedom.

responses.text: Molinists reply that counterfactuals need not be grounded in a causal sense any more than future-tense statements need be; it suffices that the person would in fact choose that way. They also argue that the grounding demand, applied strictly, would undermine knowledge of the future or the past too.

Molinists accept that God's choice of world is sovereign and inscrutable, but stress the difference: in Molinism those lost freely reject sufficient grace and would do so in any feasible world (transworld damnation is one proposal, Craig), whereas in Calvinism God withholds the grace that would have saved them.

Molinists reply that God's selecting a world does not cause the choices within it; it is the counterfactual truths themselves, which God does not control, that make the outcome what it is. That is exactly the difference from determinism.

Molinists grant that middle knowledge is a model, not a doctrine stated in Scripture, but argue that every view involves models (compatibilism, foreknowledge) and that Molinism is constrained by texts like 1 Sam 23 and Matt 11 that require counterfactual knowledge.

Molinists agree that pastoral comfort is found in Christ, not theories, but think it is legitimate faith seeking understanding to propose a coherent model, which also helps remove stumbling blocks for inquirers troubled by apparent contradictions.

Molinists clarify that the 'moments' are logical, not temporal, and that the model is compatible with a rich doctrine of union with God; it addresses a specific question about knowledge and freedom which Orthodox theology also answers (God foreknows but does not predetermine, John of Damascus).

Molinists accept that the texts show counterfactual knowledge rather than proving libertarian freedom, but argue that if humans have libertarian freedom (supported on other grounds) then such knowledge just is middle knowledge.

strawMen.strawMan: Molinism makes God dependent on creatures for his knowledge.
strawMen.correction: Molinists hold God's middle knowledge is innate and eternal, not learned from observation; God's knowledge is not caused by creatures.

strawMen.strawMan: Molinism is just Arminianism with extra steps.
strawMen.correction: Molinism is compatible with several soteriologies; some Molinists are Arminian, others (e.g. Keathley, Craig) differ on perseverance or depravity, and Molina himself was a Catholic with a strong doctrine of predestination.

positive: Offers a framework that many find reconciles sovereignty and freedom.
Influential in apologetics for the problem of evil and for questions about the unevangelised.
Has encouraged careful philosophical reflection among evangelicals.
negative: Can make soteriology seem dependent on contested philosophy.
Critics from both Calvinist and Arminian sides find it unstable.
Speculative proposals (e.g. transworld damnation) raise their own pastoral and theological questions.

adherents: Luis de Molina and many Jesuit theologians after him (some in modified congruist forms, e.g. Francisco Suárez and Robert Bellarmine)
Possibly Jacobus Arminius in part (debated by historians)
Analytic philosophers: Alvin Plantinga, Thomas Flint, Alfred Freddoso
Evangelicals: William Lane Craig, Kenneth Keathley, Kirk MacGregor, Timothy Stratton
Some Southern Baptist and non-denominational thinkers today

positions.name: Provisionism (Traditionalist Baptist)
positions.summary:
Provisionism holds that God has made a genuine provision of salvation for every person in Christ's death and that the gospel, empowered by the Holy Spirit, is itself sufficient to enable any hearer to respond in faith. Unlike Calvinism it denies that fallen people are totally unable to believe the gospel, and unlike classical Arminianism it does not posit a separate inward prevenient grace: the Spirit-inspired word is the means of enabling.

Election is understood corporately (God chose to save those in Christ, and chose Israel and the apostles for service), and believers are eternally secure. Proponents see their view as the plain reading of Scripture and as the historic conviction of most non-Calvinist Baptists.

figures.profession: English Baptist pastor, founder of the General Baptists
figures.bio: Helwys led the first Baptist congregation in England (Spitalfields, 1612) and wrote an early plea for religious liberty. The General Baptists he led held a general (universal) atonement and rejected unconditional reprobation. They are historical forerunners of non-Calvinist Baptist soteriology, though their theology was broadly Arminian and differed from modern provisionism on points such as perseverance.

figures.bio: Chaired the committee that produced the Baptist Faith and Message (1963) and wrote widely read popular expositions. His soteriology affirmed human free will and God's universal saving will alongside eternal security, representing a mid-century 'traditional' Southern Baptist outlook.

figures.name: Eric Hankins
figures.profession: Southern Baptist pastor and theologian
figures.bio: Principal drafter of the 2012 'Statement of the Traditional Southern Baptist Understanding of God's Plan of Salvation', which affirmed that every person can respond to the gospel and denied that Adam's guilt is inherited, prompting a large debate in the SBC.

figures.profession: Baptist theologian and preacher
figures.bio: Allen's large historical study argues that unlimited atonement was the majority view throughout church history, including among many Reformed theologians, and he co-edited a critique of five-point Calvinism.

figures.profession: Baptist teacher, director of apologetics for Texas Baptists, host of Soteriology 101
figures.bio: A former Calvinist whose podcast, YouTube channel and books popularised the label 'Provisionism' for this view, emphasising corporate election, the sufficiency of the gospel to enable faith, and judicial hardening in John 12 and Romans 9–11.

works.author: Leighton Flowers
works.title: The Potter’s Promise: A Biblical Defense of Traditional Soteriology

positions.context: Baptist history contains both Particular (Calvinist) and General (non-Calvinist) streams from the seventeenth century. In America, the Separate Baptist and revivalist traditions often held a modified view: universal atonement and free response alongside eternal security, a combination that is neither five-point Calvinist nor classical Arminian. Through much of the twentieth century this was the majority outlook in the Southern Baptist Convention. The resurgence of Calvinism among young Southern Baptists from the 1990s provoked a response: *Whosoever Will* (2010), the Traditional Statement (2012), and then the online ministry of Leighton Flowers, who popularised the name 'Provisionism' (late 2010s) to distinguish it from both Calvinism and Arminianism. Critics on both sides have charged it with Semi-Pelagianism, a charge its advocates reject.
claims: 1. God loves every person and has made a real provision for the salvation of all in Christ's atoning death.
2. Humans are sinful and incapable of saving themselves, but they are not born guilty of Adam's sin and are not rendered unable to respond to God's gracious, Spirit-wrought gospel appeal.
3. The gospel itself, empowered by the Holy Spirit, is God's sufficient means for enabling faith; no separate prior regeneration or universal prevenient grace is required.
4. Election in Scripture is primarily corporate (God choosing to save all who are in Christ) and vocational (choosing individuals such as Israel or the apostles for service).
5. Hardening (e.g. of Pharaoh or first-century Israel) is God's judicial response to persistent rebellion, not an eternal decree of reprobation.
6. Those who believe are regenerated and are eternally secure in Christ.

scriptures.reading: Whoever believes is not condemned; the condemnation of unbelievers is for refusing the light, which they were genuinely able to receive.
Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ: the gospel is the means by which faith is enabled.
The Gospel is written so that readers may believe: the inspired word is sufficient to produce faith.
The gospel itself is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.
God judicially blinded a generation of Israel after they had refused to believe many signs: hardening follows rebellion and serves God’s redemptive purpose.
Israel’s hardening is partial and temporary, so that salvation would come to the Gentiles and provoke Israel to jealousy, not an eternal reprobation.
Believers are chosen “in him”: election is of the body in Christ, joined by faith.
The command is not too hard or far away; Israel is called to choose life, implying ability to respond.
The son will not bear the iniquity of the father: guilt is not inherited.
God commands all people everywhere to repent, implying all can respond.

arguments.text: The repeated universal invitations and commands to repent presuppose that hearers are able to respond to them; 'ought' implies 'can' when God himself issues the call.
Paul and John attribute the enabling of faith to the word itself, not to a hidden prior regeneration.
Romans 9–11 is about Israel's corporate role and God's right to harden a rebellious Israel temporarily in order to bring Gentiles in, and the section ends with God's purpose of mercy to all.
If people cannot respond and God does not enable them, condemning them for unbelief appears unjust; Scripture grounds condemnation in refusing available light.

A majority of Baptists in America, and especially in the Southern Baptist Convention through much of the twentieth century, held this non-Calvinist, eternal-security view, as reflected in the Baptist Faith and Message.
Scripture denies that children bear the guilt of their parents, and Jesus speaks of children as belonging to the kingdom, which fits a denial of inherited guilt.

critiques.text: Scripture teaches that the natural person cannot accept the things of the Spirit and that no one can come to Christ unless the Father draws him. Provisionism's denial of inability contradicts these texts.
Provisionism is Semi-Pelagian: by locating the decisive initial move toward God in natural human capacity, it contradicts the Council of Orange (529) and the Reformation.
Classical Arminians argue that without prevenient grace, provisionism denies the depth of sin affirmed by Arminius and Wesley and comes close to Semi-Pelagianism.
Provisionism offers little account of God's providence and foreknowledge: it explains how people can respond, but not how God's specific purposes are guaranteed in history.
Lutherans, following Luther's *Bondage of the Will*, hold that the fallen will is captive and contributes nothing to conversion; provisionism overstates natural ability.

Orthodoxy agrees in rejecting inherited guilt, but considers provisionism too focused on individual decision and lacking the sacramental and ecclesial dimensions of salvation as participation in God (theosis).
Corporate election cannot account for texts that name individuals as chosen before their birth or speak of names written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.

responses.text: Provisionists reply that 1 Cor 2:14 concerns understanding spiritual wisdom, not the gospel itself (which Paul preached to unbelievers), and that the Father draws through teaching (John 6:45) and through the lifting up of the Son (John 12:32), which is the gospel.

Provisionists deny the label because they hold that no one would or could believe without God's gracious initiative in sending Christ, the gospel and the Spirit's convicting work through the word; they also point out that they do not regard Orange as binding and judge it by Scripture.

Provisionists respond that their 'enabling' is the Spirit-empowered gospel itself, which is a work of grace; the disagreement is over the mechanism, not whether grace is necessary, and they find a separate universal inward grace lacking clear exegetical support.
Many provisionists are open to Molinism or to simple foreknowledge as accounts of providence and see no conflict; their focus is soteriological rather than metaphysical.

Provisionists reply that Lutherans themselves teach that grace through Word and sacrament is resistible and offered to all, so the practical difference is narrower than it seems; they read 'dead' as separation and alienation rather than incapacity to hear.

Provisionists share the Orthodox view of ancestral sin in some respects, but regard sacramental mediation of grace as unsupported by Scripture; they understand participation in divine life as the fruit of union with Christ by faith.

Provisionists answer that individual election in Scripture is typically to service or role (Jacob as patriarch, Paul as apostle), and Rev 17:8 concerns the book of life, into which people are entered on the condition of faith (Rev 3:5 shows names can be blotted out, which some take as figurative).

strawMen.strawMan: Provisionists think people can save themselves without grace.
strawMen.correction: Provisionists affirm that salvation is entirely by grace through faith; they teach that people respond to God's gracious initiative in the gospel, which they believe the Spirit empowers.

strawMen.strawMan: Provisionism is a brand-new internet invention.
strawMen.correction: The label is recent, but the underlying view (universal atonement, ability to respond, eternal security) has a long history in Baptist and revivalist Protestantism, especially in the American South.

strawMen.strawMan: Provisionists deny original sin altogether.
strawMen.correction: Provisionists affirm that all inherit a sinful nature and environment from Adam and inevitably sin; what they deny is inherited guilt and total inability to respond to the gospel.

positive: Encourages simple, direct evangelistic appeals.
Gives a confident account of God's universal love.
Has energised biblical-theological study of Romans 9–11 and John 6 among lay Christians.
negative: Critics fear it underplays the depth of sin and the necessity of inward grace.
Online polemics have sometimes heightened tensions within the SBC.
Its relationship to historic creeds and confessions (e.g. on original sin) is debated.

adherents: Many twentieth-century Southern Baptist pastors and leaders (e.g. Herschel Hobbs)
Signatories of the 2012 Traditional Statement
Many independent Baptist and non-denominational evangelical churches
Contemporary advocates: Leighton Flowers, Eric Hankins, David L. Allen, Adam Harwood
Earlier General Baptists and Free Will Baptists are related but distinct (they generally taught prevenient grace and, often, conditional security)

positions.name: Lutheran (single predestination)
positions.summary:
Confessional Lutheranism teaches that salvation is entirely God's work: the fallen will is bound and cannot cooperate in conversion, and God's eternal election of his children is the sole cause of their salvation. Yet Lutherans deny that God predestines anyone to damnation. Christ died for all, God earnestly wills all to be saved, and grace offered through Word and sacraments is genuinely resistible: those who are lost perish by their own fault.

Lutherans refuse to reconcile these truths by logic (the so-called crux theologorum, 'why some and not others?'), insisting that the comfort of election is to be found only in Christ as he is offered in the means of grace, and that speculation about God's hidden will leads either to despair or to presumption.

figures.name: Martin Luther
figures.profession: Augustinian friar, professor at Wittenberg, reformer
figures.bio: Luther's 1525 reply to Erasmus argued that the human will is in bondage to sin and that God works all things by his immutable will, distinguishing God hidden from God preached. He later counselled troubled consciences not to speculate about predestination but to look to the wounds of Christ and their baptism.

works.title: Bound Choice, Election, and Wittenberg Theological Method

positions.context: Luther's early theology was strongly Augustinian, and his debate with Erasmus (1524–1525) put free will at the centre of the Reformation. After his death Lutherans quarrelled over Melanchthon's later language about the will (the synergist controversy) and over predestination as Reformed theology sharpened its formulations. The Formula of Concord (1577), collected in the Book of Concord (1580), settled the matter for confessional Lutherans: monergism in conversion, single predestination to salvation, universal grace, and a refusal to explain why some are saved and not others. American Lutherans revisited the question in the election controversy of the 1880s, which split the Synodical Conference.
claims: 1. Bondage of the will: in spiritual matters fallen humans can only resist God; they contribute nothing to conversion.
2. Monergism: conversion and faith are worked solely by the Holy Spirit through the means of grace (the Word and the sacraments).
3. Single predestination: God has chosen his elect to salvation in Christ, and this election is a cause of their salvation; he has predestined no one to damnation.
4. Universal grace: Christ died for all, and God earnestly desires all to be saved; his call through the Word is sincere to every hearer.
5. Resistible grace: people can and do resist the Spirit's work; the cause of damnation lies wholly in the sinner's unbelief.
6. Crux theologorum: why some are converted and others not cannot be explained; believers find assurance in Christ, baptism and the gospel, not in God's hidden counsel.

scriptures.reading: God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world: election is real, eternal and christocentric, and should be contemplated only in Christ.
Election is the cause of salvation and gives comfort to believers in suffering.
God earnestly wills all to be saved; this revealed will is to be taken at face value.
Christ wanted to gather Jerusalem and they would not: grace is resistible, and unbelief is the sole cause of loss.
No one can come unless drawn by the Father: conversion is God’s work alone.
Faith comes through the Word: God works through means, which is where election is to be sought.
God saves by the washing of regeneration: baptism is a means by which God gives new birth.
Israel’s destruction is from itself, but its help is from God (as traditionally read in the Lutheran confessions).

arguments.text: Scripture teaches both that salvation is entirely God's work and that damnation is entirely the sinner's fault; Lutheranism affirms both without reducing either to fit a logical system.
Inferring reprobation from election is a logical step Scripture does not take; reason should be captive to the Word rather than completing its doctrines by syllogism.
God's revealed will in the gospel, not his hidden will, is the place where sinners meet God, so election is preached as comfort to believers, not as a puzzle.
The Formula of Concord represents the mature consensus of the Lutheran churches after decades of controversy, carefully avoiding both synergism and double predestination.
The means of grace (preaching, baptism, the Supper) are God's instruments for giving faith, so assurance rests on objective promises rather than introspection.

critiques.text: The Lutheran view is logically unstable: if God alone converts, and he wills all to be saved, why are not all converted? Either God's will is frustrated or he does not in fact will to convert all, which implies something like reprobation.

If grace is resistible, the difference between the saved and the lost seems to lie in human non-resistance; Lutherans deny this, but their position is then incoherent. Arminianism follows the logic of universal, resistible grace consistently.
Lutheranism declines to explain how God's sovereign election coheres with resistible grace; middle knowledge could offer exactly that explanation.
Luther's bondage of the will overstates human inability; Scripture repeatedly commands people to choose, repent and believe.

Lutheran monergism and its forensic account of justification neglect the real cooperation of the person in growing into likeness with God, and baptismal regeneration in Lutheranism is held alongside a denial of human cooperation that Orthodoxy finds puzzling.
The Lutheran claim that believers may lose their faith and salvation sits uneasily with single predestination: if election is a cause of salvation, how can an elect person fall?

responses.text: Lutherans accept that the question cannot be answered by reason and regard that as the faithful position, since Scripture teaches both monergism and universal grace. They argue that Calvinism resolves the tension only by subordinating texts on God's universal will to a logical inference.

Lutherans reply that non-resistance is not a contribution to salvation (the dead do not cooperate) and that grounding salvation in human response would undercut the comfort of election; they prefer paradox to synergism.
Lutherans regard speculative models of God's knowledge as an attempt to peer into the hidden God, which Luther warned leads to terror or pride, and see no need to supplement the Word.
Lutherans answer that commands show what we ought to do, not what we can do in our own strength (Luther's argument against Erasmus), and that God gives what he commands through the Word.

Lutherans say that after conversion the renewed will does cooperate in sanctification (Formula of Concord, Article II), and Finnish Luther research (Tuomo Mannermaa) has argued that Luther himself spoke of real participation in Christ, which opens common ground with theosis.

Lutherans distinguish: the elect will be preserved, but believers who are not elect may truly believe for a time and fall away (Luke 8:13); since no one knows the hidden decree, believers are warned and comforted through the Word.

strawMen.strawMan: Lutherans are basically Calvinists on predestination.
strawMen.correction: Confessional Lutherans explicitly reject predestination to damnation and limited atonement and teach that grace is resistible.

strawMen.strawMan: Lutherans believe baptism saves automatically regardless of faith.
strawMen.correction: Lutherans teach that baptism is a means of grace that gives faith and forgiveness, but that its benefits are received by faith and can be rejected.

positive: Directs anxious consciences away from introspection to Christ and the sacraments.
Holds firmly to both sovereign grace and universal grace without rationalising either away.
Produced a rich confessional and liturgical tradition.

Its paradoxical stance can be hard to teach to lay people.

positions.name: Eastern Orthodox (synergy and theosis)
positions.summary:
Eastern Orthodoxy understands salvation as theosis: through the incarnation, death and resurrection of Christ, human beings are healed and drawn into participation in the life of God by grace. This is a lifelong process in the Church, through baptism, chrismation, the Eucharist, prayer and ascetic struggle. Salvation is synergistic: God's grace always takes the initiative and does the work, yet the free human person must cooperate, and God never overrides freedom.

Orthodoxy rejects inherited guilt: humans inherit the consequences of Adam's sin (mortality, corruption, a tendency to sin), often called ancestral sin, but not Adam's personal guilt. God foreknows but does not predetermine who will be saved; predestination is grounded in foreknowledge, and God wills all to be saved.

figures.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
figures.profession: Bishop of Alexandria, defender of Nicene faith
figures.bio: His treatise on the incarnation explains salvation as God the Word assuming human nature to restore incorruption and the divine image, culminating in the classic formula that God became human so that humans might become divine (paraphrased).

figures.name: Maximus the Confessor
figures.profession: Byzantine monk and theologian
figures.bio: Defended the doctrine that Christ has two wills (divine and human) against Monothelitism, which became the dogma of the Third Council of Constantinople (681). His theology of the will grounds Orthodox synergy: the human will, healed in Christ, freely conforms to the divine will, and deification is the goal of creation.

figures.name: John of Damascus
figures.profession: Monk and theologian at Mar Saba
figures.bio: His summary of Greek patristic doctrine taught that God foreknows all things but does not predetermine free human acts, so that predestination follows foreknowledge and virtue and vice are in our power with God's help.

works.author: John of Damascus
works.title: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith

figures.name: Vladimir Lossky
figures.profession: Russian émigré theologian in Paris
figures.bio: Lossky's influential presentation of Eastern mystical theology introduced Western readers to apophaticism, the essence–energies distinction and theosis as the heart of Orthodox soteriology, and helped shape the neo-patristic revival.

works.author: Vladimir Lossky
works.title: The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church

figures.name: John S. Romanides
figures.profession: Greek Orthodox theologian
figures.bio: His doctoral study argued that the Greek fathers did not teach inherited guilt but saw humanity's inheritance from Adam as mortality and corruption, which in turn give rise to sin; he sharply contrasted this with Augustinian theology.

positions.context: Orthodox soteriology was never shaped by a Pelagian controversy as the West's was; the Greek fathers wrote against pagan fatalism, Gnostic determinism and Manichaean dualism, and so emphasised human freedom (autexousion). John Cassian, often regarded in the West as Semi-Pelagian, is venerated as a saint in the East. When Calvinism reached the Orthodox world through Patriarch Cyril Lucaris's confession (published 1629), Orthodox synods rejected it, most fully at the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) and in the Confession of Dositheus, which affirmed that predestination is according to foreknowledge. Twentieth-century émigré theologians (Lossky, Florovsky, Meyendorff, Schmemann) and Greek theologians (Romanides) restated these themes for Western audiences.
claims: 1. The goal of salvation is theosis: participation in the divine life (God's uncreated energies), not in the divine essence.
2. Ancestral sin: humans inherit mortality and corruption from Adam, which give rise to personal sin, but not Adam's guilt.
3. Synergy: God's grace initiates, accompanies and completes salvation, while the free human person cooperates; grace never coerces.
4. Predestination according to foreknowledge: God foreknows all things but does not predetermine anyone's salvation or damnation.
5. Christ died for all and God wills all to be saved; salvation is received in the Church through faith, baptism, the Eucharist and a life of repentance.
6. Salvation is a process (I have been saved, am being saved, will be saved), and believers can fall away.

scriptures.reading: Believers become partakers of the divine nature: the scriptural basis for theosis.
Work out your salvation, for God works in you: the classic text of synergy, with God’s action and human effort together.
We are God’s co-workers (synergoi): human cooperation with God.
Christ prays that believers may be one in the Father and the Son: union with God.
Through one man death entered the world, and because of death (as many Greek fathers read eph’ hō) all sinned: inherited mortality leading to personal sin.
Believers are transformed from glory to glory into the image of the Lord: progressive deification.
Those whom God foreknew he predestined: predestination follows foreknowledge.
One must be born of water and Spirit: baptism as the beginning of new life.
Christ stands at the door and knocks: he does not force entry but awaits the free response.

arguments.text: The New Testament presents salvation as transformation into Christ's likeness and participation in God, not only acquittal.

The Greek fathers before and after Augustine (e.g. Irenaeus, Athanasius, the Cappadocians, John Chrysostom, Maximus) consistently teach free will and cooperation with grace, which reflects the apostolic tradition.
Love cannot be coerced; a God who is love invites a free response rather than determining it, and freedom is part of the divine image.
Death, not guilt, is the primary inheritance from Adam in Romans 5, and Ezekiel teaches that guilt is not transferred from father to son.
Orthodox councils explicitly rejected Calvinist predestination when it was introduced (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), showing that the Eastern tradition considered it foreign.
The incarnation itself shows synergy: Christ's human will freely conformed to the divine will (Gethsemane), and Mary's free consent preceded it.

critiques.text: Synergism compromises salvation by grace alone: if human cooperation is necessary for salvation, salvation becomes partly a human achievement, contrary to Paul.
Arminians share much with the Orthodox, but argue that Orthodox soteriology blurs justification into sanctification, so that believers lack clear assurance of acceptance with God.
Orthodoxy affirms foreknowledge without determinism but offers no account of how God's providence infallibly achieves its ends through free acts; middle knowledge would supply this.
The Orthodox emphasis on sacramental mediation and the Church as the locus of salvation adds conditions not found in the gospel's simple call to believe.
Theosis risks confusing Creator and creature, and synergy turns faith into a work; Luther's insight was that we are passive in justification, receiving Christ's righteousness as a gift.
The rejection of inherited guilt fails to account for Rom 5:18-19, where condemnation comes to all through one trespass and many were made sinners through one man's disobedience.

responses.text: Orthodox theologians reply that cooperation is not merit: grace does all the work, and the human person freely accepts and lives it out, as Phil 2:12-13 states. They regard the Western framing of grace versus works as a false alternative created by later controversies.

Orthodox answer that assurance rests on God's faithfulness and the sacramental life of the Church rather than a forensic declaration taken in isolation; humility about one's final state is itself a spiritual virtue.
Orthodox theology is generally apophatic about the mode of divine knowledge and sees no need for a philosophical theory; providence is confessed, not explained.

Orthodox respond that the New Testament itself ties baptism, the Spirit and the Eucharist to salvation (John 3:5; John 6:53; Acts 2:38; 1 Pet 3:21), and that faith is never isolated from incorporation into Christ's body.

Orthodox stress that theosis is participation in God's energies, not his essence, so the Creator–creature distinction is preserved (Palamas). They note that some Lutheran scholars (the Finnish school) see real participation in Luther himself.

Orthodox readers take Rom 5:18-19 to describe humanity's solidarity in death and corruption, from which sin inevitably arises, rather than an imputation of guilt; Ps 51:5 confesses being born into a sinful condition, not personal guilt for another's act.

strawMen.strawMan: The Orthodox believe in salvation by works.
strawMen.correction: Orthodoxy teaches that salvation is entirely God's gift; human effort is a free response to and cooperation with grace, not a means of earning it.

strawMen.strawMan: Theosis means people become God in essence, like pantheism.
strawMen.correction: Orthodox theology distinguishes God's essence (forever unknowable and unshared) from his energies (his life and activity), in which humans participate by grace.

strawMen.strawMan: Orthodoxy has no doctrine of the fall.
strawMen.correction: Orthodoxy has a strong doctrine of the fall and its consequences (death, corruption, the passions); it differs from Augustinian theology on inherited guilt.

positive: Holds together salvation, sanctification, worship and spiritual life in a unified vision.
Preserves a strong sense of human freedom and the dignity of the image of God.
Rich liturgical, ascetic and mystical traditions.
negative: Protestant critics find assurance of salvation weaker.
The concept of synergy can be misunderstood in popular piety as earning salvation.
Its differences from Western categories have made ecumenical dialogue difficult.
