readings.reading: Individual, unconditional election to salvation: God chose Jacob, passed over Esau, before they acted, and mercy depends on God alone.
God's sovereign right to define his people by faith rather than ancestry or works; Jacob and Esau represent nations and historic roles, not eternal destinies (compare Rom 9:30-32).
God's choice is sovereign and not based on works; middle knowledge explains how God can choose whom to save without determining their choices.
Corporate and vocational election: God chose Jacob's line to carry the promise and is free to harden rebellious Israel and show mercy to Gentiles who believe.
Election is wholly of grace, not works; but Lutherans refuse to infer from this a reprobation of Esau's spiritual descendants, and read the text as comfort to believers.
Read with the Greek fathers (e.g. Chrysostom's homilies on Romans) as about God's freedom in history, with God's choice according to foreknowledge of each person's disposition.
The Father's drawing is effectual: all who are drawn come and are raised up; inability is universal apart from it.
Drawing is necessary prevenient grace, and Christ draws all (John 12:32); it enables but does not compel.
Drawing is grace sufficient for salvation, given in circumstances God selects with middle knowledge.
The Father draws through his teaching and the lifted-up Son (John 6:45; John 12:32), that is, through the gospel itself.
Conversion is God's work alone through the Word; yet the drawing can be resisted, and the lost are lost by their own fault.
God draws and invites, but never forces; the person who comes cooperates with grace.
God chose particular persons in Christ before creation and predestined them to adoption, according to the purpose of his will.
Election is christocentric: God chose Christ and those who would be in him by faith (Eph 1:13).
God's choice of believers in Christ is eternal and specific, made in light of what they would freely do in the world he chose to create.
Election is of the body in Christ; individuals become part of the chosen body by believing the gospel.
Election in Christ is eternal and is to be contemplated only in Christ and his means of grace, never apart from him.
God foreordained humanity in Christ for adoption and union with himself; those who freely respond share in this calling.
Either 'all kinds of people' (in context of kings and rulers) or God's genuine desire distinct from his decree.
God truly desires each person's salvation, and Christ is a ransom for all (2:6), so grace is extended to every person.
God's universal desire is real and pursued within the constraints of what free creatures would do in feasible worlds.
God wants everyone to be saved and has made provision for all; unbelief is the only reason anyone is lost.
This is God's revealed will, which faith must take at face value even though it cannot be logically reconciled with election.
God wills all to be saved; salvation depends on the free response of each person, without which God will not save.
Those appointed (ordained) to eternal life believed: election precedes and causes faith.
The verb may be middle ('disposed themselves toward eternal life'), contrasting with those who judged themselves unworthy (13:46).
Appointment reflects God's providential arrangement of circumstances in which these Gentiles would freely believe.
Those whose hearts were rightly disposed toward eternal life, in contrast to the Jews who rejected it, believed.
Luke attributes faith to God's ordination, which Lutherans gladly affirm as comfort, without inferring the reprobation of others.
God's appointment corresponds to his foreknowledge of those who would be receptive.
Believers work out their salvation because God effectually works in them both to will and to do; God's work is the ground of human effort.
Salvation involves real cooperation enabled by grace.
God's providential work and human free effort coincide, as middle knowledge allows.
Believers are called to responsible obedience; God's work in them is the Spirit's ongoing sanctification.
This concerns sanctification after conversion, where the renewed will does cooperate (Formula of Concord, Article II).
The clearest statement of synergy: God works, and we work with him, in the process of theosis.
God is patient toward 'you' (the elect still to be gathered), or else this expresses God's preceptive will.
God genuinely wills that no person perish, which rules out unconditional reprobation.
God desires all to repent and arranges history patiently to maximise free repentance.
A plain statement of God's universal love and saving will.
God's revealed will, sincerely meant, which believers must preach to all.
God desires all to be saved and waits for their free repentance.

argumentMap.text: God unconditionally elects particular people and effectually brings them to faith.
Fallen humans are spiritually dead and unable to come unless drawn; drawing results in resurrection to life.
Paul anticipates the objection of injustice, which only makes sense if election is unconditional.
God desires all to be saved and Christ died for all; unconditional election contradicts this universal saving will.
Distinguish God's revealed desire from his decree, or read 'all' as all kinds of people in context.
The Father draws through the gospel and the lifted-up Son, who draws all; spiritual death is separation, not inability to hear.
'All' in John 12:32 means all nations (Greeks have just arrived), and new birth precedes believing in John's theology.
The Greek fathers uniformly taught predestination according to foreknowledge and free cooperation; Augustinian determinism is a Western development.
The Greek fathers addressed fatalism and Gnosticism, not Pelagianism; Scripture rather than a subset of fathers is decisive.
God elects believers in Christ and enables all hearers by resistible prevenient grace.
Scripture describes people resisting the Spirit and God lamenting their refusal.
If the same grace is given to all, the difference between believer and unbeliever lies in the human, giving ground for boasting.
Receiving a gift is not meritorious; faith excludes boasting by its very nature.
A universal inward prevenient grace distinct from the gospel lacks explicit scriptural support.
John 1:9 and John 16:8 point to a universal enlightening and convicting work of Christ and the Spirit.
God elects by choosing to actualise a world in which particular people freely believe, using middle knowledge.
Scripture attributes to God knowledge of what free agents would do in unrealised circumstances.
Grounding objection: nothing makes counterfactuals of libertarian freedom true prior to creation, so God cannot know them.
Counterfactuals need no causal ground; it suffices that the person would so choose, just as future truths need no present cause.
Election is the sole cause of salvation, yet God predestines no one to damnation and grace is resistible.
If God alone converts and wills to save all, why are not all converted? The position is logically unstable.
This is the crux theologorum: Scripture teaches both truths, and faith refuses to resolve them by speculation into God's hidden will.
Salvation is theosis received through synergy: grace initiates and completes, and the free person cooperates.
Synergy makes faith a work and theosis risks blurring Creator and creature.
Participation is in God's energies, not his essence, and cooperation is response, not merit.
The Spirit-empowered gospel is sufficient to enable any hearer to believe; election is corporate in Christ.
Without prevenient grace this position approaches Semi-Pelagianism.

title: Have the miraculous gifts ceased?
question: Have the miraculous gifts ceased?
intro:
The New Testament describes a range of spiritual gifts, among them prophecy, speaking in tongues and their interpretation, healings and miracles, given to believers in the first-century church. Christians agree that the Holy Spirit indwells and gifts every believer today. They disagree about whether these particular gifts were meant only for the apostolic foundation of the church, or whether they continue until Christ returns.

The question became a live debate with the rise of Pentecostalism (1906) and the charismatic renewal, but earlier writers had already reflected on the apparent rarity of such gifts. Three main positions are presented here: cessationism, continuationism, and the mediating 'open but cautious' view, each with its exegesis of key texts, its reading of church history, and its critics' objections and replies.

positions.name: Cessationism
positions.summary:
Cessationism holds that the miraculous or 'sign' gifts of the Spirit described in the New Testament (especially apostleship, prophecy as new revelation, tongues and their interpretation, and gifts of healing and miracles exercised at will) belonged to the founding era of the church and ceased with the apostles and the completion of the New Testament. God still answers prayer, heals and works providentially, but he no longer distributes revelatory or sign-working gifts to individuals as in the apostolic age.

There are several kinds of cessationist argument. Some (Warfield) emphasise that miracles authenticated the apostles as bearers of revelation. Others (Gaffin) emphasise that prophecy and tongues were revelatory and belonged to the once-for-all foundation of the church, now completed in Scripture. A minority read 'the perfect' of 1 Cor 13:10 as the completed canon; many cessationists, including Gaffin, do not rely on that reading.

figures.name: B. B. Warfield
figures.profession: Professor of theology at Princeton Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield, the leading Old Princeton theologian, gave the classic modern form of cessationism in lectures published as *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918). He argued that miraculous gifts were the credentials of the apostles, conferred through them, and so ended with the generation on whom they laid hands; he then critically surveyed patristic, medieval Catholic, Irvingite, faith-healing and mind-cure claims, judging them unreliable or explicable otherwise.

figures.name: Richard B. Gaffin Jr.
figures.profession: Professor of biblical and systematic theology, Westminster Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Gaffin's argument centres on the history of redemption: Pentecost, like the cross and resurrection, is a once-for-all event, and the apostles and prophets form the foundation of the church (Eph 2:20). Revelatory gifts belonged to that foundation and ceased when it was laid. He represents cessationism in the Four Views volume and interprets 'the perfect' in 1 Cor 13:10 as the return of Christ.

works.author: Richard B. Gaffin Jr.
works.title: A Cessationist View, in Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views

figures.name: John MacArthur
figures.profession: Pastor of Grace Community Church, Sun Valley, California
figures.bio: Influential pastor and broadcaster whose books and 2013 'Strange Fire' conference strongly criticised the charismatic movement for doctrinal error, fraud and abuses, and defended cessationism to a wide evangelical audience.

figures.name: O. Palmer Robertson
figures.profession: Reformed Old Testament scholar
figures.bio: Robertson argued that New Testament prophecy and tongues were revelatory and therefore ceased with the closing of the canon, and wrote specifically against Wayne Grudem's view of fallible New Testament prophecy.

figures.name: Thomas R. Schreiner
figures.profession: New Testament scholar, Southern Baptist Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Schreiner, who previously held a more open view, set out a moderate cessationism, arguing that prophecy in the New Testament is infallible revelation and that the apostolic foundation argument shows its cessation, while conceding that the exegetical case from 1 Cor 13 is not decisive.

works.author: Thomas R. Schreiner
works.title: Spiritual Gifts: What They Are and Why They Matter

positions.context: Many patristic and Reformation writers observed that the extraordinary gifts of the apostolic age had become rare or absent in their own day (Chrysostom, the early Augustine, Calvin), though they rarely formulated a doctrine of cessation. Protestant polemic against Catholic miracle claims, which were used to validate Roman doctrine, encouraged the argument that miracles had ceased. Warfield's *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918) systematised the case in response to Catholic claims, Irvingite tongues, the faith-healing movement and Christian Science. Twentieth-century Pentecostalism and the charismatic renewal made the question urgent across evangelicalism, and Gaffin, MacArthur and others developed the case.
claims: 1. The apostles were a unique, unrepeatable office, and their signs authenticated them as bearers of revelation.
2. The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets; once that foundation was laid, the revelatory gifts that belonged to it ceased.
3. Prophecy and tongues (with interpretation) were forms of new revelation; with the completion of the New Testament, Scripture is the sufficient and final word.
4. Miraculous sign gifts were concentrated in redemptive-historical epochs (Moses, Elijah and Elisha, Christ and the apostles) rather than spread evenly through history.
5. Some cessationists read 'the perfect' (1 Cor 13:10) as the completed canon or matured church; others read it as the second coming and rest the case on other arguments.
6. God still heals and acts powerfully in answer to prayer, but not through individuals possessing the apostolic sign gifts.

scriptures.reading: The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets; a foundation is laid once, so the foundational gifts do not continue.
The message was confirmed (past tense) to us by those who heard the Lord, with God bearing witness through signs and gifts: miracles authenticated the first generation of witnesses.
The signs of a true apostle were performed among the Corinthians: miracles were credentials of apostleship, not common possessions.

Prophecy, tongues and knowledge will pass away when the perfect comes. Some cessationists read the perfect as the completed revelation of Scripture; others read it as the end but note tongues are said to cease of themselves.
The faith was once for all delivered to the saints: revelation is complete.
God has spoken finally in his Son, whose revelation the apostles transmitted.
The Spirit’s gifts in Samaria came through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, which Warfield took to show that the gifts were conferred through the apostles.
Tongues were a sign to unbelieving Israel, fulfilling Isa 28:11, tied to the transition from the old covenant to the new.
Nothing is to be added to the words of the prophecy, which many cessationists apply by extension to the closed canon.

arguments.text: The foundation argument: apostles and prophets are named together as the church's foundation; since apostles are not perpetuated, neither is the prophetic gift with which they are paired.
Miracles in Scripture cluster around new stages of revelation and function to authenticate God's messengers, which implies they wane when the revelation is complete.
If prophecy and tongues continue as revelation, the sufficiency of Scripture is compromised; if they continue as fallible, non-revelatory impressions, they are not the New Testament gifts.

Already in the late fourth century Chrysostom said the gifts of 1 Cor 12 were no longer occurring and that this made the passage obscure (*Homilies on 1 Corinthians* 29), and the early Augustine said tongues and such signs had passed away.
The church's rejection of Montanism's 'New Prophecy' (second century) shows an early sense that new prophetic revelation was not to be expected or received.

Contemporary claims of tongues, healings and prophecy do not match the New Testament phenomena (known languages, instantaneous and complete healings, infallible prophecy), so they should not be identified with the apostolic gifts.
In the later New Testament letters, healing is no longer exercised at will even by Paul's associates, suggesting the gifts were already receding.

critiques.text: Warfield's core thesis, that miraculous gifts were conferred only through apostolic hands, does not fit the evidence: the Spirit fell on Cornelius's household without apostolic hands, Ananias (not an apostle) laid hands on Paul, and Paul expects the whole Corinthian church to exercise gifts.

Jon Ruthven argued that Warfield's case depended more on Scottish Common Sense philosophy and anti-Catholic, anti-faith-healing polemic than on exegesis, and that his principle that miracles serve only to accredit revelation is not how the New Testament describes them (they also express compassion and the arrival of the kingdom).

Church history does not show cessation: Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 2.32.4) reports healings, exorcisms, visions, prophetic speech and even raisings of the dead in his churches, and (5.6.1) speaks of brothers with prophetic gifts who speak in all kinds of languages; Justin Martyr says prophetic gifts remained among Christians (*Dialogue with Trypho* 82).

Augustine changed his mind. Early on he said such miracles were not permitted to continue (*On True Religion* 25.47) and that tongues had passed away (*Homilies on 1 John* 6.10), but later he catalogued many healings at Hippo and elsewhere (*City of God* 22.8) and qualified his earlier remark in his *Retractations*.

The 'perfect' in 1 Cor 13:10 cannot be the canon: Paul says that when it comes we will see face to face and know fully even as we are fully known, which describes the return of Christ, not the closing of the New Testament.

No New Testament text states that the gifts will cease before Christ's return; the foundation argument is an inference, and Paul commands the church not to forbid tongues and to earnestly desire prophecy.

Even if the gifts were concentrated in the apostolic age, God's sovereignty means we cannot rule out his giving them again, especially in missionary frontiers; cessationism claims more than Scripture warrants.

Pentecost in Acts 2:17-18 inaugurates 'the last days', which run until Christ returns; Peter applies Joel's promise of prophecy to all of God's people in this whole era, including 'all who are far off'.

responses.text: Many modern cessationists concede that Warfield's 'apostolic hands' thesis was overstated and no longer rely on it, resting instead on the foundation argument (Gaffin) and the revelatory nature of prophecy and tongues. Warfield himself treated Cornelius as an exceptional, redemptive-historical event marking the Gentile Pentecost.

Cessationists reply that a polemical setting does not invalidate an argument, and that the accrediting function of miracles is explicit (Heb 2:3-4; John 20:30-31; 2 Cor 12:12) even if they also show compassion. The question is whether the gifts as a category were intended to continue.

Cessationists answer that the second-century reports are early and may reflect the tail end of the apostolic generation's gifts (Warfield's view), or may describe answered prayer rather than gifts in the apostolic sense; they also note that reports decline noticeably in the third century before rising again with relic cults in the fourth.

Cessationists note that the miracles of *City of God* 22.8 are largely associated with the relics of Stephen and with prayer, not individuals exercising gifts, which is consistent with their view that God still heals in answer to prayer. Warfield argued that such relic miracles are historically dubious and served developing cultic practice.

Many cessationists, including Gaffin and Schreiner, agree that the perfect is the parousia and do not base cessationism on this verse. They argue the passage teaches only that the gifts will certainly end by the parousia, not that they must continue until it, and that other texts show they ended earlier.

Cessationists agree no verse states the timing directly, but argue that a cumulative case (foundation, authentication, revelatory character, sufficiency of Scripture, historical observation) is legitimate, just as the closing of the canon is itself inferred rather than stated. Paul's commands addressed a church in the foundational era.

Cessationists acknowledge that God is free to work miracles at any time, but distinguish this from the claim that the church today should expect individuals to possess revelatory and sign gifts as a normal part of church life.

Cessationists reply that Pentecost fulfils Joel in the once-for-all outpouring of the Spirit, and that what continues is the gift of the Spirit himself to all believers (Acts 2:38), not every phenomenon that accompanied his first coming.

strawMen.strawMan: Cessationists do not believe God does miracles today.
strawMen.correction: Cessationists affirm that God heals and works wonders in answer to prayer; they deny that the specific gifts of revelation and sign-working given to individuals continue.

strawMen.strawMan: Cessationists believe the Holy Spirit is no longer active.
strawMen.correction: Cessationists teach the ongoing indwelling, illumination, sanctification and gifting (teaching, service, mercy, leadership) of the Spirit in every believer.

strawMen.strawMan: Cessationism rests entirely on reading 1 Cor 13:10 as the canon.
strawMen.correction: Many leading cessationists reject that reading and rely on the foundation, authentication and sufficiency arguments instead.

positions.name: Continuationism
positions.summary:
Continuationism holds that all the gifts of the Spirit listed in the New Testament, including prophecy, tongues, interpretation, healing and miracles, remain available to the church until Christ returns. The 'last days' inaugurated at Pentecost continue throughout the church age, and nothing in Scripture says the gifts would be withdrawn earlier.

Many non-Pentecostal continuationists (e.g. Grudem, Storms) distinguish New Testament congregational prophecy, which is a human report of something God spontaneously brings to mind and must be tested, from the authoritative revelation of the apostles and Scripture, so that continuing gifts do not threaten the closed canon. Pentecostals and charismatics share the conviction of continuing gifts while often adding distinctive teaching on Spirit baptism.

positions.context: Claims of continuing gifts appear in the second and third centuries (Irenaeus, Justin, Tertullian), were complicated by the Montanist controversy, and recur in various renewal movements. The modern movement began with Pentecostalism (Topeka, 1901; Azusa Street, Los Angeles, 1906), spread into mainline and Catholic churches through the charismatic renewal (from 1960), and among evangelicals through the 'Third Wave' associated with John Wimber in the 1980s. Reformed and evangelical theologians such as D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones (in sermons published as *Joy Unspeakable*, 1984), Wayne Grudem and Sam Storms argued from Scripture that the gifts had not ceased. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians now number in the hundreds of millions, especially in the Global South.
claims: 1. The gifts of the Spirit are given for the common good and the building up of the church throughout the church age.
2. 'The perfect' of 1 Cor 13:10 is the state brought about by Christ's return, when we will see face to face; until then, prophecy and tongues continue.
3. The 'last days' of Joel's prophecy, fulfilled at Pentecost, extend to Christ's return and to all generations of believers.
4. New Testament congregational prophecy is not equal in authority to Scripture; it must be tested and does not add to the canon.
5. Miracles express God's compassion and the presence of the kingdom, not merely the authentication of apostles.
6. The gifts should be pursued eagerly and exercised in an orderly way under the authority of Scripture.

scriptures.reading: The gifts cease when the perfect comes and we see face to face, which is Christ’s return; until then they remain.
Pursue love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy: a standing command to the church.
Earnestly desire to prophesy and do not forbid speaking in tongues.
In the last days God pours out his Spirit on all flesh and they prophesy; the last days span the whole church age.
The promise is for you, your children and all who are far off: later generations are included.
Gifts including healing, miracles, prophecy and tongues are given to ordinary members for the common good.
Do not quench the Spirit or despise prophecies, but test everything: prophecy is fallible and must be weighed.
The Corinthians lack no gift as they wait for the revealing of Christ: gifts are linked to the time until his return.
Christ gave gifted ministers until we all attain to the unity of the faith and mature manhood, a goal not yet reached.
Prophecy is to be exercised in proportion to faith, alongside ordinary gifts like serving and giving.

arguments.text: No passage teaches that the gifts would cease before the parousia; 1 Cor 13:8-12 ties their cessation to seeing face to face.
Gifts in 1 Corinthians are given to ordinary church members for edification, not only to apostles for authentication.
New Testament prophecy is regularly evaluated and can be partially mistaken in detail (Agabus), which shows it is a different kind of authority from Scripture and does not threaten the canon.

Second-century writers report ongoing gifts: Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 2.32.4 and 5.6.1) and Justin (*Dialogue with Trypho* 82); Augustine later recorded many healings (*City of God* 22.8), reversing his earlier statements.
Warfield's arguments have been seriously criticised (Ruthven, Deere), and many cessationists no longer use his apostolic-hands thesis.
The cessationist 'foundation' argument proves too much: if prophecy ceased because prophets were foundational, then evangelists and teachers, listed with them in Eph 4:11, should also have ceased.
Contemporary documentation of healings and other phenomena (collected by Keener and others) shows such experiences are widespread, especially in missionary contexts.

critiques.text: If prophecy continues, either it is revelation from God, in which case it is infallible and adds to Scripture, or it is fallible, in which case it is not the New Testament gift; Grudem's 'fallible prophecy' is a new category with no basis in Scripture, which condemns false prophecy.
Eph 2:20 places prophets in the foundation alongside apostles; foundations are laid once. Prophecy therefore belonged to the founding era.
Modern tongues are generally not known human languages, unlike Acts 2, and modern healings are seldom instantaneous and complete as in the Gospels and Acts, so the phenomena are not the same.
Heb 2:3-4 speaks of the gospel being confirmed in the past by signs given to the first generation of hearers, implying their attesting role was complete.
The rise of excesses, false prophecies, prosperity teaching and abuses in charismatic movements shows the danger of claiming continuing revelatory gifts.

Continuationists sometimes identify modern phenomena too quickly with the New Testament gifts and treat them as normal expectations for every believer, without sufficient discernment or attention to the diversity of the gifts.

Carson and others argue that charismatic theology often rests on doctrines (Spirit baptism as a second blessing, tongues as initial evidence) that are poorly supported by 1 Cor 12–14, even if the gifts themselves continue.

responses.text: Grudem and Storms reply that the New Testament itself treats congregational prophecy as subject to evaluation (1 Cor 14:29; 1 Thess 5:20-21), distinguishes it from apostolic authority (1 Cor 14:37-38), and records a prophecy accurate in substance but inexact in detail (Acts 21:11). Deut 18 concerns those claiming to speak with divine authority in the Lord's name.

Continuationists note that Eph 2:20 may refer to apostles who are also prophets (one group) or to the specific prophets of the apostolic circle, and that 1 Cor 12–14 describes a wider congregational gift of prophecy that is not foundational.

Continuationists reply that 1 Cor 14:2 describes tongues that no one understands, speaking mysteries to God, which suggests tongues need not be known human languages; and that healings in the New Testament also varied (Mark 8:22-25 is gradual) and did not always happen (2 Tim 4:20).
Continuationists say the verse describes how the readers received the message, not that signs must stop; Hebrews is silent about whether they continued.

Continuationists such as Storms and Grudem openly criticise abuses and the prosperity gospel, but argue that misuse calls for biblical regulation (1 Cor 14), not prohibition; Paul corrected Corinthian disorder without forbidding the gifts.

Thoughtful continuationists agree that not all speak in tongues (1 Cor 12:30), that experiences must be tested, and that the gifts should be desired rather than demanded. They accept caution as a virtue but regard the default stance of the New Testament as eager pursuit.

Third Wave continuationists (Wimber, Grudem, Storms) largely agree and reject subsequence and initial-evidence teaching; they argue for continuing gifts on exegetical grounds independent of classical Pentecostal theology.

strawMen.strawMan: Continuationists believe modern prophecies are equal to Scripture.
strawMen.correction: Most evangelical continuationists explicitly deny this, teaching that Scripture is closed and uniquely authoritative and that prophecy must be tested by it.

strawMen.strawMan: Continuationism means endorsing everything done in the name of the Spirit.
strawMen.correction: Continuationist scholars frequently critique fraud, manipulation and prosperity teaching, and call for the orderly exercise of gifts.

strawMen.strawMan: Continuationists are all Pentecostals who teach a second blessing.
strawMen.correction: Many continuationists (Reformed charismatics, Third Wave) reject subsequence and initial-evidence doctrines.

positions.name: Open but cautious
positions.summary:
The 'open but cautious' position holds that Scripture does not teach that the miraculous gifts have ceased, so Christians should be open to God giving them today; but it is cautious about identifying contemporary phenomena with the New Testament gifts, about the theology often attached to them, and about practices that can lead to error or division.

The label comes from Robert L. Saucy's contribution to *Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views* (ed. Wayne Grudem, 1996). D. A. Carson's exegetical study *Showing the Spirit* (1987), which rejects the main cessationist arguments while criticising charismatic theology, is often grouped with it.

positions.context: As the charismatic renewal spread into evangelical churches in the 1960s–1980s, many leaders found neither strict cessationism nor full charismatic practice persuasive. British evangelicals (Stott, Packer) navigated tensions in the Church of England, and in America the Third Wave prompted fresh exegetical work. The Four Views volume (1996) presented four positions: cessationist (Gaffin), open but cautious (Saucy), Third Wave (Storms) and Pentecostal/charismatic (Douglas Oss), with mutual responses. Many evangelical churches today effectively operate in this space.
claims: 1. Scripture nowhere clearly teaches that the miraculous gifts would cease before Christ's return.
2. The miraculous gifts were concentrated in the apostolic era, and we should not expect them in the same frequency or form as a normal pattern.
3. Claims of contemporary gifts must be carefully tested, and many phenomena may not correspond to the New Testament gifts.
4. Charismatic doctrines such as subsequence and initial evidence are not well supported by Scripture.
5. Believers should be open to God working miraculously, especially in pioneering mission, while prioritising Scripture, love and the ordinary means of grace.
6. The question should not divide churches; unity and charity should govern disagreements.

scriptures.reading: The perfect is the parousia, so the passage does not teach early cessation; but it also does not guarantee that the gifts will be common.
Do not quench the Spirit, but test everything: the balance of openness and caution in a single text.
Test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out: a call to caution.
The Spirit distributes gifts as he wills; neither cessationists nor charismatics can dictate what he must do.
Not all speak in tongues or work miracles, so no gift is a universal sign of Spirit baptism.
Gifts without love are nothing: love is the controlling priority.
Miracles had a special attesting role with the first witnesses, supporting the expectation that they were concentrated then.
Some who prophesy and do mighty works in Jesus’ name are rejected, a warning against equating spiritual power with faithfulness.

arguments.text: The exegetical case for cessation (especially from 1 Cor 13:10) does not hold, so cessationism goes beyond what Scripture says.
Miraculous activity in the Bible is uneven, clustering around key epochs, so it is reasonable to expect less frequent miracles after the apostolic era without asserting their cessation.

Church history shows both continuing reports (Irenaeus, Augustine's *City of God* 22.8) and a marked decline and testimony that some gifts were rare (Chrysostom's *Homilies on 1 Corinthians* 29), which fits neither a clean cessation nor uniform continuation.
The Montanist crisis shows the danger of unchecked prophetic claims, and the church's response illustrates the need for testing.
Openness avoids limiting God's sovereignty, and caution protects the sufficiency of Scripture and the health of the church.
Because both sides agree on the essentials of the gospel, a mediating position allows cooperation and mutual correction rather than division.

critiques.text: If the gifts may still be given, the 'cautious' stance is inconsistent: Paul commands believers to earnestly desire them, not merely to tolerate them. Either they continue and should be sought, or they have ceased.

In practice the position lacks criteria: without a principled reason for cessation, it cannot explain why prophecy should not be practised in every church, and it often drifts into charismatic practice.
The caution can quench the Spirit: by discouraging expectation and practice, churches effectively become cessationist in experience, which Paul warns against.

The claim that miracles were concentrated in the apostolic era rests on argument from silence; the Gospels and Acts also show ordinary disciples (the seventy, Stephen, Philip, Ananias) performing miracles.
Church history largely supports cessation: Chrysostom testifies the gifts were no longer occurring, the early Augustine said so as well, and Montanism showed what new prophecy led to.
Calling a position 'cautious' implies continuationists are incautious; many continuationists equally emphasise testing and order.

responses.text: Saucy replies that openness can be paired with caution about what is presented as a gift; desiring gifts is compatible with recognising that the Spirit distributes them as he wills and that the apostolic-era frequency need not be normative.

Open-but-cautious advocates respond that Scripture's tests (agreement with apostolic teaching, edification, order, love) provide criteria, and that sufficiency of Scripture is maintained when any claimed prophecy is subordinate to it.

The open-but-cautious view accepts the warning but notes that the same passage requires testing everything (1 Thess 5:21), and that Paul himself regulated the gifts in Corinth; caution is a form of obedience, not quenching.
Saucy grants this, but notes that those examples are still tied to the founding period and the immediate circle of the apostles; the claim is about relative frequency, not impossibility.

The open-but-cautious view replies that the historical evidence is mixed: Irenaeus reports gifts in his day, Augustine later catalogued healings, and many reports exist across history; history counsels caution but does not prove cessation.
Advocates agree that thoughtful continuationists are careful; the label describes a different default expectation (less frequent, not normative) rather than a charge of recklessness.

strawMen.strawMan: Open but cautious is just fence-sitting with no convictions.
strawMen.correction: It holds specific exegetical convictions: that Scripture does not teach cessation, that miracles were concentrated in the apostolic era, and that charismatic distinctives are unsupported.

strawMen.strawMan: Open-but-cautious believers are functionally cessationists.
strawMen.correction: Many such churches pray for healing, welcome reports of God's working and allow for prophecy-like gifts, but do not make them central or normative.

'The perfect' is the parousia, when we see face to face (13:12); until then prophecy and tongues continue.
'The perfect' is the parousia, so this text does not teach cessation; it is silent on frequency in the meantime.
Apostles and prophets are the once-laid foundation; prophecy, like apostleship, ended when the foundation was complete.
Refers to apostle-prophets or the founding prophets only; congregational prophecy in 1 Cor 14 is a different, non-foundational gift.
Shows the unique role of the founding apostles and prophets, but does not by itself settle whether lesser forms of prophecy continue.
Signs confirmed the message through the first hearers (past tense); their attesting purpose has been fulfilled.
Describes how the readers received the gospel; it does not say signs stopped.
Indicates miracles were concentrated around the first witnesses, supporting an expectation of fewer, not none.
Miracles were 'signs of an apostle', distinguishing apostles from ordinary believers.
Paul's apostolic signs were distinctive in scale or character, but 1 Cor 12 shows non-apostles also had miraculous gifts.
Shows a special concentration of signs in apostolic ministry.
Joel's prophecy was fulfilled in the once-for-all outpouring of Pentecost; what continues is the gift of the Spirit himself.
The 'last days' run to Christ's return, so the promise of prophecy extends to all generations.
The last days indeed continue, so prophecy is possible, but the passage does not specify its frequency or form.
Addressed to the church while the foundational gifts were still active; not a command for the church after the canon's completion.
A standing command: earnestly desire prophecy and do not forbid tongues.

Prophecy in Thessalonica was revelation during the apostolic era; testing applied then and Scripture is now the test.
Shows prophecy was ongoing, fallible and subject to testing, fitting continuing congregational prophecy.

timeline.title: Didache on testing prophets
timeline.note: The *Didache* (c. 100, date debated) gives instructions for receiving and testing travelling prophets (ch. 11).

timeline.title: Justin Martyr's *Dialogue with Trypho*
timeline.note: Justin says prophetic gifts remain among Christians (ch. 82); dated c. 155–160.

timeline.title: Montanism (New Prophecy)
timeline.note: Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla prophesy in Phrygia (c. 156–172, dates debated); the movement is rejected by Asian synods, deepening suspicion of new prophecy. Tertullian later joined it (c. 207).

timeline.title: Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*
timeline.note: Reports healings, exorcisms, prophecy and even raisings of the dead (2.32.4) and brothers speaking in all languages through the Spirit (5.6.1); written c. 180.

timeline.title: Augustine's early cessationist remarks
timeline.note: In *On True Religion* 25.47 (c. 390) Augustine says such miracles were not allowed to continue to his time; similar statements on tongues in *Homilies on 1 John* 6.10 (c. 407).

timeline.title: Chrysostom's *Homilies on 1 Corinthians*
timeline.note: Homily 29 says the passage on gifts is obscure because the phenomena no longer occur (preached in Antioch c. 392, date debated).

timeline.title: Augustine's *City of God* 22.8
timeline.note: Augustine catalogues healings at Hippo and elsewhere, many linked to Stephen's relics, and later qualifies his earlier remarks in the *Retractations* (c. 427, 1.13.7; locator needs verification).

timeline.note: William J. Seymour leads the Los Angeles revival that spreads Pentecostalism worldwide (following Topeka, 1901).

timeline.title: Warfield's *Counterfeit Miracles*

Eph 2:20 concerns founding prophets; congregational prophecy in 1 Cor 14 is a distinct, non-foundational gift.

Scripture does not teach cessation, but the gifts were concentrated in the apostolic era and claims today must be carefully tested.
